Why Powhatan tolerated the English
column2: Powhatan considered the colonists a nuisance but let them survive because English trade goods and weapons helped him strengthen his rule and fend off Piedmont tribes.

column1: How Spain colonized the Southwest and Florida
column2: Spain held its northern borderlands with scattered military garrisons, cattle ranches, and missions staffed by Dominican and Franciscan priests.

column1: Why Spain's northern colonies stayed small
column2: New Mexico and Florida were poor and dangerous, so few Spaniards settled there, and the colonies survived mainly as missions and military buffers.

column1: The lesson of Acoma
column2: The Acoma massacre taught the Pueblos that resistance brought terror, but Spanish brutality also destroyed the cooperation New Mexico needed to prosper.

column1: Why Spain kept New Mexico
column2: The Franciscans persuaded the Crown to keep unprofitable New Mexico by arguing that abandoning baptized Indians would betray Catholic duty.

column1: The causes of the Pueblo Revolt
column2: Forced labor, disease, famine, Apache raids, and Spanish repression of Pueblo religion united the Pueblos to rise against Spanish rule.

column1: How mercantilism drove colonization
column2: Mercantilism encouraged European monarchs to sponsor colonies because colonies supplied raw materials, bought finished goods, and increased royal revenue and power.

column1: The significance of the Virginia Company
column2: The Virginia Company planted England's first permanent colony, and its land and political reforms laid the foundation for Virginia's growth before its failures led to royal rule.

column1: Why Jamestown nearly failed
column2: Jamestown nearly collapsed because gentlemen refused to work, settlers lacked farming skills, disease and brackish water spread, and colonists demanded food from Indians.

column1: How Virginia's reforms attracted settlers
column2: The headright system, an elected assembly, and relaxed martial law attracted migrants and investment, allowing Virginia's tobacco economy to expand.

column1: The significance of the headright system
column2: The headright system rewarded planters who imported laborers with more land, so it drove the flood of indentured servants and the growth of large tobacco plantations.

column1: The consequences of the tobacco boom
column2: Tobacco profits drove relentless seizure of Indian land and constant demand for labor, causing Indian wars and dependence on indentured servants before slavery prevailed.

column1: The cycle of Indian wars in the Chesapeake
column2: The Chesapeake Indians, organized in an effective confederacy, went to war whenever a new generation of men came of age, in 1622, 1644, and 1675.

column1: How Maryland differed from Virginia
column2: Maryland combined family proprietary rule, Catholic leadership, and toleration for all Christians, making it both a Catholic refuge and Virginia's tobacco rival.

column1: How England took greater control of its colonies
column2: England tightened control by making Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia royal colonies, passing the Navigation Acts, and adopting Charles II's consistent colonial policy.

column1: The causes of Bacon's Rebellion
column2: Falling tobacco prices, landless freed servants, Indian conflict, and exclusion from power united frontier farmers and ambitious gentlemen against Berkeley's government.

column1: How the Navigation Acts affected the Chesapeake
column2: The Navigation Acts strengthened England's mercantilist empire but restricted Chesapeake trade and deepened planters' distress as tobacco prices fell.

column1: How slavery evolved in the early South
column2: In the early Chesapeake some blacks were free or indentured and had more rights, but harsh slave codes followed once larger numbers arrived directly from West Africa.

column1: How slavery united white society
column2: As slavery replaced servitude, fear of the growing black population drew whites of all classes and religions into a racist consensus led by a new gentry.

column1: How the slave trade transformed West Africa
column2: Slave trading enriched African rulers who built stronger states, while warfare, kidnapping, famine, and disease drew interior communities into bondage.

column1: The scale of Atlantic slavery
column2: The Atlantic slave trade carried far more Africans than Europeans to the Americas, making African workers central to every plantation economy.

column1: The characteristics of the Caribbean sugar economy
column2: Sugar turned the English Caribbean into deadly, black-majority slave societies of great wealth, and Britain valued the West Indies as its most valuable American possession.

column1: How Caribbean planters controlled enslaved people
column2: Caribbean blacks never had a period of rough frontier equality, because sugar planters enacted brutal slave laws early to control the slaves who soon dominated the islands.

column1: The economic origins of South Carolina
column2: Land scarcity on Barbados sent planters to found South Carolina, which grew rich exporting rice and later indigo with the skilled labor of a black majority.

column1: How African expertise built South Carolina's rice economy
column2: South Carolina's rice wealth depended on enslaved Africans' knowledge of rice growing, yet white fear of the black majority produced Caribbean-style slave codes.

column1: How Carolina's Indian slave trade reshaped the Southeast
column2: Carolina traders turned Indian slavery into a major business, devastating Florida's missions and neighboring peoples until the Yamasee War ended the trade.

column1: The result of the Yamasee War
column2: The Yamasee War nearly destroyed South Carolina and ended proprietary rule, and the colony won only with Cherokee help, while southeastern confederacies learned to balance rival empires.

column1: The trustees' plan for Georgia
column2: Georgia's trustees banned slavery and liquor and limited landholding so the colony could be a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge of small farms.

column1: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia differed
column2: South Carolina grew rich on rice and slaves, North Carolina stayed a poor colony of small farms and naval stores, and Georgia began as a slave-free buffer and refuge.

column1: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia were alike
column2: All three colonies began under proprietors or trustees, ended as royal colonies, and ultimately depended on plantation agriculture and enslaved labor.

column1: How Europeans changed Native American societies in the South
column2: Europeans spread disease, forced Indians into missions, seized land for tobacco, and drew them into the slave trade, wrecking older ways of life across the South.

column1: The common pattern of southern colonies
column2: Southern colonies shared staple-crop economies, close ties to English merchants, inequality among whites, racial slavery, and Indian dispossession.

column1: The staple crops of the southern colonies
column2: The Chesapeake specialized in tobacco, South Carolina in rice and indigo, and the Caribbean in sugar, tying each region's wealth to coerced labor.

column1: Why Indian-settler relations differed across the southern colonies
column2: Disease and slavery had nearly erased Caribbean Indians before English settlement, Chesapeake peoples fought back through a strong confederacy, and South Carolina drew many Indians into trading pelts and captives.
